title: What's this? — three kinds of nouns
goal: Name the things around you, read a noun's gender straight from its last letter, and point at three distances that Bosnian keeps apart — this, that, and that over there.
bekal: guess the gender of almost any noun from its last letter
point at things with *ovaj / ova / ovo* and pick the right distance between *ovo*, *to*, and *ono*
make adjectives agree with their noun: *mali sto, mala soba, malo pismo*

notes: **Ovo, to, ono — three distances, not two.** English has "this" and "that"; Bosnian adds one more level (like old English *yonder*). *Ovo* = this, near the speaker. *To* = that, near the listener or just mentioned. *Ono* = that over there, far from both — which is why Budi uses *ono* for the stove across the room, and Emir answers *ono je peć*.

**When introducing something, always the neuter form — whatever the thing.** *Ovo je džezva* even though *džezva* is feminine; *Ovo je sto* even though *sto* is masculine; *Ovo su fildžani* for plural. A big relief: "this is…" never requires you to know the noun's gender. It's completely different when the pointing word is attached to a noun: then it must agree — *ovaj sto*, *ova stolica*, *ovo pismo*.

**Adjectives agree too.** Follow the trail through the dialogue: *soba* is feminine, so *mala je, svijetla je, lijepa je*. *Sto* is masculine, so *mali sto*. *Fildžani* is plural, so *lijepi su*. That's why you must note the gender with every word from day one — not for the sake of a table, but for the adjective endings that show up in nearly every sentence.

**Things are "he" or "she" too.** *Je li i on moj?* — Budi says *on* (he) about a table, because *sto* is masculine. Bosnian has no separate "it" for objects; everything is *on*, *ona*, or *ono*, following the word's gender. *Gdje je kafa? — Ona je na stolu.*

**The Bosnian kitchen speaks Turkish.** *Kašika* (spoon), *tanjir* (plate), *džezva*, *fildžan*, *čaršaf* (bedsheet), *sahan* (pot), *jorgan* (quilt) — all Ottoman inheritances. *Bit će* in the last line is a small preview of the future tense, which comes in unit 19; for now learn it whole as "it will be".

grammars.title: Three kinds of nouns — read from the last letter
body: This is the most important lesson of the first ten units, and luckily one of the easiest: for almost every word, **the last letter tells you the gender straight away**. Nothing to memorize word by word, as in German or French.
after: **The rule holds about nine times out of ten.** The rest fall into just two groups, and both make sense. First, a handful of words end in a consonant but are **feminine**: *noć* (night), *stvar* (thing), *ljubav* (love), *riječ* (word), *pomoć* (help), *večer* (evening). Learn these six now and you're practically done.

**Second, words ending in *-a* that refer to men are treated as masculine for meaning**: *tata* (dad), *kolega*, *sudija* (judge), *vođa* (leader). The noun's endings follow the feminine pattern, but the adjective is masculine: *moj kolega je nov*. This rarely trips anyone up, since the meaning makes it obvious.

**Masculine adjectives have two shapes.** *Ovaj mali sto* — but *sto je malen* for some adjectives. The *-i* forms (*mali, novi, dobri*) are used when attached to a noun that is already known; the bare forms (*mal, nov, dobar*) are used standing after *biti*: *Sto je nov.* At A1 this difference rarely causes misunderstanding — pick either, then notice how native speakers use them.

**The ten-second habit:** say every new noun together with its pointing word, never alone. Not *soba*, but *ova soba*. Not *prozor*, but *ovaj prozor*. That way the gender is stored with the word, not in a separate list you have to look up later.

grammars.title: Ovaj, taj, onaj — pointing at three distances
body: All three change to match their noun, just like adjectives. The table looks dense, but there is only one pattern: change the front, keep the ending.

after: ***To* is the form used most in everyday speech.** If you're unsure which of the three to use, use *to* — it's almost always natural. *Šta je to?* is a question you will ask hundreds of times in Sarajevo, and nobody will correct it.

**Two different jobs — don't mix them up.** When the pointing word stands alone as the subject ("this is…"), it is always **neuter singular**: *Ovo je moja sestra. Ovo su moji roditelji.* When it is attached to a noun, it **agrees with the noun**: *Ova knjiga je nova. Ovi fildžani su lijepi.*

**Don't be confused by seeing *ona* and *oni* twice.** The same word works as a personal pronoun (*ona* = she, *oni* = they) and as the far pointer (*ona knjiga* = that book over there). What decides the meaning is simply whether a noun follows.

**One little word people forget: *evo*.** It means "here you go, here it is" — used when handing something over or showing something: *Evo kafe! Evo, ovdje je frižider.* Its siblings: *eto* (there you go, that's it) and *eno* (there it is, over there).

sections.title: Stvari u kući — things in the house

blocks.text: This list is not for learning all at once. Read it while looking around your own room, and say each word with its pointing word — *ovaj prozor*, *ova stolica*, *ovo ogledalo*. A gender learned while pointing at a real object sticks far better than one memorized from a column.

Notice *vrata* (door): it is plural in form, and always plural — *vrata su otvorena* (the door is open), never singular. Bosnian has a handful of words like this: *vrata* (door), *kola* (car), *leđa* (back), *novine* (newspaper), *naočale* (glasses). English does something similar with "scissors" and "trousers" — the verb is plural there too.

blocks.title: Four sentences that unlock almost any new word
items: ***Šta je ovo?*** — "What's this?" The most productive sentence in any language. Point, ask, repeat the answer aloud, done.
***Kako se kaže "…" na bosanskom?*** — "How do you say '…' in Bosnian?" Use this when you know the English word but not the Bosnian one.
***Šta znači "…"?*** — "What does '…' mean?" The reverse, for a word you've just heard.
***Možete li ponoviti, molim vas?*** — "Could you repeat that, please?" Keep this one in your pocket; you'll use it more often than the other three.
